title: 24. FDE / Customer Engineering
description: Turing S4 core: decomposition case studies (5-step framework), client-simulation role-plays, and behavioral-embedded-in-technical prompts. The single biggest FDE filter — ~40% pass rate per Exponent.

24.1 Decomposition (5-step): Step 1: Clarify the actual problem (ask, don't assume)
Step 2: Identify stakeholders + success metric owner
Step 3: Map inputs — data availability, freshness, ownership
Step 4: Decompose into 2-4 workstreams, sequence by risk/value
Anti-pattern: jumping to solution before clarifying (top rejection reason)
24.2 Client Simulation: Ownership language ('I will', not 'the team will')
Acknowledge valid points before pushing back
Present explicit trade-off menu, not one option
Written follow-up after every verbal commitment
24.3 Behavioral-in-Technical (60-sec STA: Pattern: 'You've mentioned X — can you give an example?'
Handle rapid-fire behavioral without breaking flow
Return to code after story completes
Interviewers embed these to test composure

questions.prompt: A large city wants to reduce 911 response times using call data, traffic patterns, and ambulance GPS. Walk through your first 60 minutes with the customer.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: which failure mode matters most — dispatch delay, routing, staging?
Stakeholders: dispatch, EMS ops, city IT, unions, civil-rights review; identify success-metric owner
Map inputs: GPS refresh, call taxonomy, traffic API terms, PII rules
Decompose 2-4 workstreams sequenced by risk/value
Walking-skeleton MVP: one district, one call type, dashboard-only (no automated dispatch)
Names failure modes and rollback (bad recommendation harms response)

questions.modelAnswer: First 10 min: ask which metric moves — avg response time, tail P95, or equity by ZIP. Identify accountable exec. Next 20 min: map data — GPS refresh interval, call classifier fidelity, traffic API terms. Next 15 min: decompose into (1) baseline dashboard, (2) staging-location optimizer, (3) dispatch assist. Sequence: (1) first (no risk), (2) as recommendation, (3) gated behind human confirmation. Last 15 min: 4-week MVP scope = dashboard for one borough, one call category, no automated action.

questions.prompt: Regional bank has 3 acquired fraud-detection systems with inconsistent labels. Scope a 90-day plan to unify.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: keep all 3 running or replace? cost of FP vs FN? regulatory reporting
Data reconciliation: unified label schema, historical relabeling, gold-set curation
Doesn't propose 'one big model' Day 1 — phased approach
Weeks 1-30 shadow+eval; 30-60 pick winner/ensemble; 60-90 cutover with rollback
Compliance + audit story (Model Risk Management doc)
Explicit rollback + kill switch per system

questions.modelAnswer: Week 1: interview each fraud team, get 6mo labeled data, agree unified label set with regulator input. Wk 2-6: replay all 3 on unified holdout; measure precision/recall/economic impact per segment. Wk 6-10: choose ensemble strategy. Wk 10-12: shadow. Wk 12+: cutover behind per-region flag with immediate rollback. MRM doc for compliance.

questions.prompt: Pharma researcher wants AI assistant to query internal compound + trial data. Legal, IP, compliance nervous.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: who is allowed to see which data (compound access, active trials)
Deployment in customer VPC only; no third-party for retrieval or generation
Full audit log: user, query, retrieved docs, response, timestamp
PII/patient redaction pre-embedding
Read-only assistant to start; structured tools later
Ethics + IP review board loop before wider rollout

questions.modelAnswer: MVP = read-only Q&A over public + Phase-completed compound docs. Data-classification tags flow into retrieval filters keyed on user role. Self-hosted embedding + LLM in customer VPC. Immutable audit store. Legal + IP review corpus before onboarding. Phase 2 adds Phase-active data with attestation. No autonomous actions in v1.

questions.prompt: Logistics company wants AI agent to reroute shipments using SAP + weather APIs + 500 warehouse managers.

rubric.criterion: Clarify success: cost / on-time / manager time saved
Human-in-the-loop above impact threshold
Phased: shadow → advisory → semi-auto → auto
Observability + kill-switch per warehouse
Change-management for managers
Explicit failure modes named

questions.modelAnswer: Start with 5 warehouses in shadow: agent produces recommendations, manager sees but acts normally. Compare for 30 days. Advance to advisory (one-click accept). Then auto-approve low-dollar reroutes; escalate high-dollar. Per-warehouse toggle. Weekly office hours with managers to feed corrections into eval set.

questions.prompt: Insurer wants automated summarization of 30M historical claims for adjusters. Regulation varies by state.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: summary attached to claim (regulated) or adjuster's tool (advisory)?
Per-state config drives allowed fields, PHI, retention
Eval set built WITH adjusters
Hallucination guardrails: cite spans, refuse if uncertain
Pilot state, then per-state review
Feedback loop into evaluation

questions.modelAnswer: Advisory tool. Adjuster sees summary alongside raw claim always. Model requires cited spans; UI shows citations. State-config drives allowed fields. Golden eval of 200 claims labeled by seniors. Start in one small state; expand after clean eval + adjuster satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Healthcare client deployed your AI platform 90 days ago. Adoption is 12%. Diagnose + plan.

rubric.criterion: Refuses to jump to 'more training' — investigates first
Talks to non-adopters directly, segmented by role
Product telemetry: activation funnel, drop-off points
Compares heavy vs light vs non-users — what's different?
Names 2-3 hypotheses with cheap tests, ranked
Escalation plan if workflow/political, not product

questions.modelAnswer: Wk 1: pull funnel; interview 5 non + 5 heavy users. Hypotheses: (a) workflow doesn't include tool at right moment, (b) results aren't trusted, (c) IT policy blocks flow. Rank cheapest test first. Test 1: shadow heavy user, find handoff. Test 2: trust survey. Wk 2: prioritize biggest gap, ship 1-week fix. Report to sponsoring exec with 30/60/90 recovery plan.

questions.prompt: You deployed AI agent at a bank. Three weeks in, outputs violate undisclosed internal policies.

rubric.criterion: Immediately pauses affected functions rather than debate scope
Gets actual policies documented in writing
Retroactive audit: past violations flagged + remediated
Adds guardrails (policy-check pass) + eval set update
Post-incident review with client, no blame
Escalation: legal + hiring manager early

questions.modelAnswer: Hour 0: kill affected function, notify. Hour 4: interview client compliance to list every applicable policy. Day 2: retroactive audit + remediation. Day 3-7: policy-check gate on every output; incorporate examples into eval set. Wk 2: post-incident with client — process failure was ours (didn't ask for policies up front) — propose new intake checklist.

questions.prompt: Novel prompt — walk through 5-step framework: 'A city wants an AI to spot potholes from streetlight camera footage.'

rubric.criterion: Step 1 clarify: which cameras, resolution, response ownership
Step 2 stakeholders: city IT, DoT, camera-owning agency, residents, unions, budget owner
Step 3 inputs: video access legality, retention, night quality, FP tolerance
Step 4 decompose: detection, triage/ranking, dispatch integration
Step 5 skeleton: 10 cameras, daily batch, dashboard for DoT, no dispatch automation v1
Measure success as potholes-fixed-per-dollar, not detection accuracy

questions.modelAnswer: See rubric — narrate each step aloud, ending with scoped 4-week MVP that produces a dashboard reviewed by DoT before any autonomous action.

questions.prompt: Hospital chain wants clinical decision support that references their internal SOPs, drug DBs, and patient EHRs. Scope.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: advisory or automated? HIPAA + BAA + PHI handling
Deploy inside VPC; self-hosted models
Retrieval scoped by user role (nurse vs attending vs specialist)
Citations mandatory + refusal on low confidence
Clinical validation loop with attending physicians
Phased: one specialty, one hospital, then expand

questions.modelAnswer: Advisory only, physician-in-loop. VPC deploy with BAA in place. Retrieval filters by user_role + specialty. Every response cites SOP section + drug DB entry. Refusal threshold on similarity. Clinical validation panel reviews weekly sample. Pilot in ED at one hospital before expansion.

questions.prompt: Retailer with 5k stores wants demand forecasting integrated with legacy SAP + 12 data sources. Ambiguous ask.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: which SKU class matters most? Which time horizon?
Landing zone → silver → gold data pattern
Baseline forecast (naive/seasonal) before ML
Feedback loop: forecast → actual → error attribution
Rollout: one region, one SKU class first

questions.modelAnswer: Ask which SKU class + time horizon has biggest business impact. S3 raw → dbt silver → feature store gold. Baseline = last-year same-week; measure error. ML only if it beats baseline meaningfully. Feedback loop compares forecast to actual weekly, attributing error. Pilot in one region, apparel class, 8-week horizon.

questions.prompt: Telecom call center wants AI to reduce average handle time on customer complaints. What do you do first?

rubric.criterion: Ask what drives handle time — clarify before proposing
Listen to 20 recorded calls before touching code
Segment complaint types + prioritize by volume × handle time
MVP: agent assist (suggested responses) not full automation
Union / rep-input consulted early

questions.modelAnswer: First: sit with 3 agents for a shift and listen to 20 real calls. Segment complaints; find the 3 that account for 70% of handle time. MVP = agent-assist popup with suggested response draft; agent edits + sends. Not full automation. Consult union rep early — this affects their work. Measure reduction in handle time for those 3 types.

questions.prompt: Financial services client wants auto-generation of monthly compliance reports. Regulators require signed accuracy.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: 'signed accuracy' means human signs, or system attests?
System generates DRAFT; compliance officer reviews + signs
Audit trail: every input source + generation step logged immutably
Regression testing on historical reports the officer would have written
Version control on templates + regulatory rule changes

questions.modelAnswer: System generates draft; compliance officer reviews and signs — automation of draft, not accuracy. Every input pulled from source system logged with checksums. Officer diff view shows what changed vs last month. Backtest against 24 months of prior reports for parity. Templates versioned; new regulatory rule triggers PR review.

questions.prompt: Novel: an airport wants to predict security-line wait times and re-staff lanes dynamically. Walk through.

rubric.criterion: Clarify: predict for whom (passengers via app, or ops for staffing)?
Stakeholders: TSA, airport ops, airlines, unions
Inputs: existing wait sensors, flight schedules, boarding-pass scans, historical patterns
Decompose: (a) prediction model, (b) staffing optimizer, (c) passenger-facing display
MVP: dashboard for ops, no automated staffing changes v1
Failure: bad prediction → misallocated staff → longer waits — must be reversible

questions.modelAnswer: Clarify: are we predicting for passenger app or for ops-team staffing? Different UX + accuracy targets. Stakeholders: TSA (federal), airport ops, airlines, TSA union. Inputs: sensor wait times, flight schedules, boarding-pass scan volume. Decompose: (1) prediction model for next-hour wait, (2) staffing recommendation, (3) public-facing display. MVP = dashboard for ops (rec + why); no auto staffing until 8 weeks of validation. Kill switch per terminal.

questions.prompt: Client asks for a model that auto-approves loan applications. What's your response as an FDE?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't accept scope as stated — pushes back on 'auto-approve'
Names fair-lending regulation, adverse-action notice requirements
Proposes decision-support (score + reason codes) with human decisioner
Bias audit + model risk management doc
Rejection reason must be legally defensible + explainable

questions.modelAnswer: Stop and clarify — 'auto-approve' has fair-lending, ECOA, and adverse-action implications that require an accountable human decisioner in most jurisdictions. Recommend: decision-support model outputs score + top 3 reason codes; underwriter approves/denies + signs. Include bias audit across protected classes, MRM doc. Rejections need reason codes the applicant can appeal.

questions.prompt: CEO says 'we want AI to make us more efficient.' What do you say back in the meeting?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't nod along — asks for specifics
Reframes: which team, which workflow, what metric moves?
Offers to run a 2-week discovery to surface top 3 opportunities
Frames as customer-friendly, not gatekeeping
Sets a written outcome for the discovery

questions.modelAnswer: That's a great signal — before we start building, I want to be useful. Can I propose a 2-week discovery? I'll talk to your ops, sales, and finance leads, watch a few workflows, and come back with 3 concrete opportunities ranked by impact × feasibility. That way we invest engineering time where it moves the number, and you can pick which ones matter. Sound reasonable?

questions.prompt: Deployment slipped 3 weeks. Client CTO is on the call, visibly frustrated. First 5 minutes.

rubric.criterion: Own it upfront: 'I take responsibility'
State fact concisely — what slipped, why, what's confirmed vs uncertain
Ask 1-2 diagnostic questions about their operational pressure
Present REVISED plan with dates, not vague promises
Offer explicit trade-off options (narrower scope now vs current scope later)
Set next check-in and written summary

questions.modelAnswer: I want to own this. Three weeks behind on X due to [cause]. Y confirmed complete; Z still at risk. Before I lay out recovery — what's most exposed on your side? Two options: (a) cut scope to top 3 flows, ship in 1 week, (b) hold scope, land 2.5 weeks late fully verified. I'll send written summary within the hour and be on this call Fri 3pm until shipped.

questions.prompt: Client insists on a feature that would bypass their own governance policy. Push back without breaking relationship.

rubric.criterion: Acknowledges underlying need before objecting
Names the specific policy in plain terms
Explains concrete risk (audit fail, breach, reputational)
Offers 1-2 alternatives that meet same need within policy
Escalates to their compliance team if needed

questions.modelAnswer: I hear you — you need X so your team can move faster on Y. Building it that way bypasses your data-classification policy Z. If we ship it and your auditor finds it, it's a bigger cleanup than the time we're saving. Two alternatives: [A within policy], or [B with scoped compliance exception]. I'll set up 20 min with your compliance lead this week to walk through B — usually the fastest legit path.

questions.prompt: Non-technical VP wants a written guarantee of 100% accuracy from the LLM. Respond.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't sign the guarantee — under any framing
Explains why 100% isn't achievable, in plain language
Reframes: what business outcome are they protecting?
Proposes measurable SLOs + audit + HITL for critical paths
Offers reversibility: rollback + kill switch

questions.modelAnswer: I understand this needs to be safe enough to defend to your board. I can't sign 100% — no LLM system is 100%; anyone who signs is lying. What I CAN commit: audit trail of every response, 99.X% task-success SLO measured weekly, human review on high-impact actions, one-click rollback. Can we walk through your 2-3 riskiest scenarios and design guardrails around those?

questions.prompt: Client IT will not grant production credentials needed for your integration. Unblock without circumventing security.

rubric.criterion: Asks WHY, not just what's needed
Proposes least-privilege, time-bound, rotated credentials
Works through their SSO/vault (Vault, AWS SM, CyberArk)
Phased: read-only first, write later after review
Willing to defer prod step to preserve trust + policy

questions.modelAnswer: Fair — prod creds are exactly what should be hard to get. What's the specific policy they're worried about? If it's blast-radius, we can start with read-only creds scoped to 2 tables, rotated weekly, checked out via your Vault. If still too much, shadow in lower environment for 2 weeks, ask for prod only after zero drift. Who from security should I loop in?

questions.prompt: Client calls during live demo — errors in front of their executive team. Handle it.

rubric.criterion: Composure — no panicking, no blame
Owns it in the moment; execs hear operator not victim
Buys time: switch to known-good scenario or fallback
Commits to written follow-up within stated window
Does NOT hotfix live in front of the exec team

questions.modelAnswer: Live: 'That's a real error — I own it. Let's continue with [known-good scenario] so you see the end-to-end feel. I'll be back to you by EOD with the fix and cause.' Off-call: root-cause fast, write short summary email to exec + champion by close of business. Don't hotfix in the demo.

questions.prompt: Client demands a six-week feature in three days.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't say yes to keep peace
Asks what problem the deadline solves — real ask is often smaller
Offers smaller-in-3-days + full-in-6-weeks split
Names what breaks if compressed further

questions.modelAnswer: Help me understand what's driving 3 days — specific meeting, external commitment, internal deadline? If we compress, I can ship [thinnest slice that solves that specific thing] in 3 days, full feature stays 6 weeks. Squeezing further either misses the deadline anyway or ships something we rebuild. Which sounds better?

questions.prompt: You deployed a fix 2 hours ago. Client reports same problem is back. Losing confidence.

rubric.criterion: Owns the confidence problem, not just the bug
Doesn't debate whether it's 'the same' — treats perception as data
Rolls back if uncertain rather than shipping fix #2
Names the process gap that let fix #1 ship without verification
Written post-mortem within 24 hours

questions.modelAnswer: You're right — two fixes in two hours would erode my trust too. Rolling back now while I confirm root cause; better stable than fast. Process gap: shipped based on my-side repro without verifying customer environment path. Post-mortem to you EOD tomorrow: (1) actual cause, (2) verification that would have caught it, (3) process changes so it doesn't happen a third time.

questions.prompt: Two teams inside the client (Data + IT) are blocking each other; your project stalled between them.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't pick a side
Names standoff to exec sponsor before it's a delivery issue
Proposes joint 30-min meeting with specific decision on agenda
Offers technical middle path both can accept
Documents decision so it doesn't reopen

questions.modelAnswer: Sponsor: 'Blocked between Data and IT on X — neither has veto but neither moves without other. I'll set 30-min Thursday with one decision on the agenda: [specific choice]. Bringing a proposal that gives both sides most of what they want. Can you attend and back the decision that comes out?' Then run to written decision; distribute same day.

questions.prompt: Non-technical CFO asks why the LLM gives different answers to the same question on different runs.

rubric.criterion: Uses lay analogy without patronizing
Explains sampling / temperature plainly
States what CAN be deterministic and what can't
Connects to business impact: report, audit, compliance
Offers mitigation: guardrail + human review + logging

questions.modelAnswer: Like asking a fast writer to draft the same memo twice — same instructions, fresh draft with slightly different phrasing. We can turn creativity down to nearly zero so answers become very consistent, but two runs may still differ in small ways because the math is nondeterministic on GPU hardware. For anything auditable, we log inputs/outputs, add automated checks, and have a human sign critical decisions.

questions.prompt: Six weeks in, client keeps adding 'just one more thing' requests. Ship date slipping. Reset expectations.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't just say no — acknowledges every ask is legitimate
Reframes: 'each ask costs time from the primary goal'
Introduces or reinforces a change-request process
Offers explicit trade: 'we can add X if we drop Y or extend N days'
Weekly written prioritization ritual going forward

questions.modelAnswer: Every request you've made is reasonable — I want to acknowledge that first. Problem: each one costs 2-3 days from the primary deploy, which is now 3 weeks late. Proposal: from today, new asks go into a 'v1.1' bucket that we tackle after primary ships. If something is truly must-have for v1, it displaces something already scoped — we'd pick together. Weekly 15-min prioritization call to keep clean. Sound OK?

questions.prompt: Your executive champion at the client just left the company. New exec doesn't know your project. What do you do?

rubric.criterion: Acknowledges the risk immediately — projects die without a champion
Requests intro meeting within a week
Prepares one-page: what, why, ROI-to-date, ask
Identifies backup champions across the org
Doesn't wait for them to reach out

questions.modelAnswer: Real risk — projects die without an internal champion. Reach out to the new exec's chief-of-staff within 48 hours to request 30 min introduction. Prep a one-pager: what we're building, business problem, ROI-to-date, what I need from them (nothing initially — just visibility). Identify 2-3 backup relationships (director, ops lead) so we're not single-threaded again.

questions.prompt: Client says 'your model is wrong' but on investigation the model output is correct — their data is stale. Handle.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't just say 'your data is wrong' — even if true
Shows the trace: input → retrieval → output with citations
Points at the stale-data root cause diplomatically
Offers to help fix the upstream data issue
Preserves relationship

questions.modelAnswer: Let me pull the exact trace for that query. [shows] The model retrieved doc X from source Y — the answer matches what's in Y. Looks like Y was last updated 6 weeks ago; the actual truth changed 3 weeks ago in system Z. The model doesn't have Z wired in yet. Two options: (a) add Z to retrieval this sprint, (b) I'll surface a 'source freshness' warning in the UI so users see when data may be stale. Want to walk through together?

questions.prompt: One department head at the client openly dislikes your project (sees it as threat to their team). How do you handle when you must work with them?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't try to convert them by argument
Understands the underlying threat perception — meets 1:1 first
Finds where your project creates value for their team specifically
Involves them in a decision (co-authorship builds ownership)
Escalates only if actively sabotaging

questions.modelAnswer: Ask for 30 min 1:1, no agenda, just listen. Usually the threat is 'this replaces my team' — validate the concern (it may be legitimate). Then find one thing your project can uniquely enable for their team (e.g. their reporting gets easier). Invite them to co-own a design decision so they have visible authorship. If they still actively block, that's an exec-sponsor conversation, but 90% of the time this defuses.

questions.prompt: Project done. Client wants you to hand off to their in-house team. Their team has no LangGraph experience. Plan.

rubric.criterion: Multi-week handoff, not one meeting
Comprehensive docs: architecture, runbook, on-call playbook
Shadowing period both directions (them watching you, then you watching them)
Ramp-down: less involvement over time, not cliff
Named point-of-contact after handoff for questions

questions.modelAnswer: 4-week ramp. Wk 1: written architecture doc + runbook + on-call playbook; 2 walkthrough sessions. Wk 2: they take low-stakes tickets, I pair. Wk 3: they take all tickets, I review. Wk 4: they're primary, I'm on-call backup. After: monthly office hours for 3 months. Explicit named point-of-contact on my side for escalations.

questions.prompt: Contract renewal in 30 days. Signals are cool. What's your play?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't wait for renewal meeting — reaches out proactively
1:1 with each key stakeholder to hear unfiltered feedback
Documents delivered value with numbers
Names any promised-but-not-delivered items honestly
Proposes next 90 days concretely, tied to their priorities

questions.modelAnswer: Don't wait. Request 30 min with the exec sponsor + separate 30s with 2-3 users to hear unfiltered feedback. Prep before: written impact summary with hard numbers (X hours saved, Y errors caught, $Z prevented). Own anything I promised but didn't deliver. Come with proposed next 90 days tied to whatever came up in the user 1:1s. If it's still cool after that, ask directly: what would change your mind on renewal? Handle answer.

questions.prompt: You're 20 min into a coding problem. Interviewer stops you: 'That reminds me — tell me about a time you took ownership of a problem that wasn't technically yours.' Deliver in under 60 seconds and get back to code.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 seconds — timed
Full STAR compressed: 1 sentence each S / T / A / R
Specific: real project, real numbers
Smooth transition back to code without losing thread

questions.modelAnswer: S: Onboarding funnel was dropping 40% at step 3. T: Data team owned metrics but I owned the frontend — I took the diagnosis. A: Session-replay analysis, found 3 friction points, prototyped fixes in a week, A/B tested one at a time. R: 40% → 18% drop-off in 6 weeks, ~$300k ARR added. [BEAT] OK, back to where we were — I was iterating on the hash map lookup, let me continue…

questions.prompt: Mid-way through a system design whiteboard, interviewer: 'Describe a time you handled a difficult stakeholder.' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 seconds
Doesn't villainize the stakeholder
Names underlying need
Concrete action + measurable result
Returns to whiteboard cleanly

questions.modelAnswer: S: PM kept escalating we were 'unresponsive.' T: I owned turning that around in a quarter. A: 1:1 to hear what they actually needed — turned out predictability, not speed — introduced weekly written status + decision log. R: Zero escalations that quarter; format adopted by 2 other teams. [BEAT] OK, back to the design — I was on the API gateway component…

questions.prompt: 'Tell me about a technical decision you reversed.' 60 sec, mid-interview.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Intellectual honesty — no spin
New evidence that changed the mind
How the reversal was handled cleanly

questions.modelAnswer: S: I chose Kafka for a low-throughput event bus. T: Two months in, usage was 10 events/sec, ops burden disproportionate. A: Proposed SQS; migrated writers behind feature flag, drained Kafka, decommissioned. R: 60% infra cost drop, on-call load fell. Learned to insist on 90-day cost/ops review on default infra picks.

questions.prompt: 'Cross-team alignment without formal authority — example?' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Names outcome that required alignment
Concrete tactics — writing, 1:1s, proposal doc
Result: real change

questions.modelAnswer: S: Three teams owned pieces of billing pipeline with incompatible retry semantics. T: I wanted single strategy but couldn't mandate. A: Wrote 2-page proposal, ran review with all three leads; agreed on shared idempotency key + backoff lib. R: End-to-end retry bugs ~5/mo → 0 for two quarters running. Written proposal beat meetings.

questions.prompt: 'Tell me about a deployment that failed.' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Real failure, not humble brag
Owns share — 'I' not 'we/they'
Concrete process change since

questions.modelAnswer: S: Led a migration that took the API down 40 min. T: I owned cutover. A: Had rollback but hadn't rehearsed it; when we needed it, rollback also failed. Recovered by manually reverting DNS. R: 40-min outage. Since then every migration I rehearse rollback in staging before green-lighting cutover. Last quarter's PG16 migration had a rehearsed rollback we used cleanly — 3-min hiccup instead of 40.

questions.prompt: 'Time you told a customer no and held the line.' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Real principle behind the 'no'
Acknowledged valid underlying need
Offered alternatives
Relationship survived (evidence)

questions.modelAnswer: S: Customer asked us to disable audit logging on a specific report because it was noisy. T: I owned the answer. A: Acknowledged the pain — noise makes signals invisible — but disabling audit was compliance risk to their own regulator. Offered log filtering + cleaner UI. R: They accepted; their compliance team later thanked me directly when the regulator asked for that log.

questions.prompt: 'Why FDE, not regular SWE?' 60 sec, in the middle of a technical round.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Connects to specific past customer-facing work
Names what you value: ambiguity, ownership, direct impact
Avoids generic 'hard problems' / 'AI is cool'

questions.modelAnswer: Last three years I've either sat with customers or built for internal teams with the same feedback loop. What I like: problems start messy — real data, real politics, real deadlines — and you end with something that actually works in their environment, not just mine. FDE makes that the whole job. I'm looking at [company] specifically because [specific reason tied to their real work].

questions.prompt: 'Pattern you spotted across multiple customers or projects.' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Concrete pattern — not 'customers want speed'
How you validated it (data or repeated obs)
What changed as a result

questions.modelAnswer: S: Across five customers deploying our webhook integration, same failure at month 2 — their receiver started dropping traffic under load. T: I owned pattern reports to product. A: Documented pattern with logs from all five, proposed a client-side rate-limiter as opt-in library. R: Shipped in v2.3; new customers stopped hitting it. FDEs are earliest signal source for product; role only works if we bring patterns back inside.

questions.prompt: 'Shipping under a tight deadline with imperfect info.' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Tradeoffs made explicitly
Communicated uncertainty during, not after
Followed up on the shortcuts

questions.modelAnswer: S: Investor demo in 5 days with a broken data pipeline. T: I owned getting credible end-to-end story ready. A: Scoped demo to two accounts we knew were clean; documented the shortcut; ran pipeline nightly (not real-time) for demo; told lead + CEO exactly what we had shipped. R: Demo landed the round; filled in real-time piece next sprint. Naming shortcuts publicly makes them repayable.

questions.prompt: 'Fully remote project across time zones — how did you make it work?' 60 sec.

rubric.criterion: Under 60 sec
Specific async practices
Wrote down normally-verbal things
Shipped outcome that would have failed with poor async

questions.modelAnswer: S: Four engineers, three timezones, 6-week deadline, no shared meeting time > 2h/day. T: I was tech lead. A: Every task had written design doc reviewed async; daily standup was a written thread; decisions logged in one doc; I overlapped 1h with each timezone daily. R: Shipped on time, zero re-work from misalignment. Async-by-default is faster once the team accepts writing over meetings.
